Reference experiment, at Jack Heart's pointer ("Claude Haiku is the better experiment to check against"): Manabot experiments/haiku-mtg183.md (completed 2026-10-27; code added in Manabot commit d7b98a487c, "Add OpenRouter evaluation and publish Haiku-MTG-183 results"; config configs/llm/openrouter-haiku-high.json; runner described in docs/llm.md "Hosted models (OpenRouter)"). What it did, to design against: 100 games, Claude Haiku 5.5 via OpenRouter against the final MTG-183 policy (196,482 parameters, sampled on CPU with one Torch thread); the game process called the API directly, no inference server; up to ten games overlapped while waiting on the network; 120-second decision deadline; one protocol repair then a recorded seeded fallback; HTTP or provider failures stop, and no game is retried or overwritten; spend stops at $2 per game and $50 per campaign, checked before each hosted decision from OpenRouter's reported cost ("launch/decision stop thresholds, not hard billing caps"); median 1.386 s and p95 8.780 s per decision; $37.08 reported for 33,477 decisions. The model is recorded as slug plus serving provider, with the note "Hosted slugs are not immutable weights". Credentials came from the environment only; nothing forwarded a key to a rented machine. So per-token cost is visible to the author's code through the provider's reported usage; the design question is how that reaches Etude's limits and records.
